newsitem.title: UK: U.S. data fail to cut dollar free of tired ranges.
newsitem.headline: U.S. data fail to cut dollar free of tired ranges.

text.p: The dollar inched higher after the U.S. data it had spent the whole week waiting for, but ended a listless European day little moved from its position a week ago.

U.S. September retail sales rose 0.7 percent, surprising a market braced for 0.2, but the blow was softened by a revision converting August's 0.2 percent increase to a 0.2 percent fall and by a jump in the car sales component, analysts said.
September producer prices rose 0.2 percent versus the forecast 0.3, while the core rate was up 0.3 percent.
The dollar was quoted at 1.5307/12 marks by 1500 GMT, a touch higher than late Thursday's level here of 1.5294/04.
Last Friday's European close saw the U.S. currency trading at 1.5296/02, and it has spent this week wedged in a one-pfennig range between 1.5225 and 1.5325.
Dollar/yen, which has passed the week trapped between 110.90 and 111.95, stood at 111.67/77 yen at 1515 GMT versus 111.24/29 in late Europe yesterday.
Analysts said the inflation data backed the Federal Reserve's decision to leave rates steady at its last meeting.
"It's making people feel a bit more confident that there isn't a near-term U.S. inflation threat and consequently the dollar's rising," said Stephen King at HSBC James Capel.
"But I can't say the dollar's been the main area of interest during the course of the day," said King, who is Capel's deputy chief economist in London.

The undoubted centre of attention was sterling, which powered to 20-month highs as the market rode the wave of euphoria gripping the ruling Conservatives after an upbeat party conference which exuded a new-found party unity.

Sterling was quoted at 2.4127/32 marks by 1537 GMT compared to late Thursday's 2.3940/45, with the cross dragging cable to a new 1996 high. It firmed around a cent from yesterday's closing levels to $1.5758/68.

"The big unanswered question is whether this new-found unity will last past the weekend. There are a lot of issues that haven't gone away," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy in London.

Looking ahead for the dollar, Capel's King saw little on the horizon to spur it out of well-worn ranges, as nerves ahead of the U.S. elections capped the upside and a mark undermined by European monetary union speculation leant support.
But others were more sanguine.
"Dollar/yen is setting up for a potential test of the upside next week up to the highs (near 112)," said one trader.
That should drag dollar/mark upwards, he added.
The market will focus next week on U.S. September consumer price data, due Wednesday, in the light of today's PPI numbers.
Also of significance will be Friday's U.S. trade figures for August, forecast to show the deficit narrowing to $9.2 billion from $11.7 billion last time.
Other figures out today showed the University of Michigan consumer sentiment index for October at a preliminary 94.8 compared to a final 94.7 in September.
-- Abigail Levene, London Newsroom +44 171 542 8968
